The market stall’s canvas roof snapped in the wind off the Ascendant Run, and Carys’s hand hovered above the folded note I still held between my fingers. I could not make myself release it. The youth’s binding still flickered in my mind, the elder’s demand still pressed at the back of my throat, and every breath I took tasted of the spiralgrass crushed underfoot.

Carys leaned closer, her voice low so the other vendors would not hear. “If you keep it any longer the ink will smudge from your sweat. Give it over.”

My thumb traced the edge of the parchment once more. The note carried the only proof we had that the bloodline geas had been tampered with before the youth ever stepped into the circle. Handing it across meant someone else would know what Julian had already risked to shield us both.

I let the paper slide from my palm. Carys took it without flourish, tucking it beneath a bolt of dyed river-silk as though it were nothing more than a price list. Her heel tapped once against the stall leg before she shifted her weight.

Behind us the crowd thickened at the next stall. A voice rose above the rest—clear, carrying, the sort that belonged to someone used to being listened to. The council messenger who had arrived at the clearing was reading from a sealed letter, the one that had been intercepted with the token from Julian’s house. The words carried across the market air.

“…three wishes offered in the old manner, each bound to the same bloodline, each paid for in secret. The first for safety of the line, the second for the return of what was lost, the third—”

The rest was lost beneath the sudden rush of voices. People turned. Some laughed, thinking it theater. Others went still, because the old manner meant sacrifice that could not be undone. A fly settled on the back of my wrist and stayed there.

Carys’s fingers tightened on the silk. “They will trace it back,” she said. “You need to decide which one you can afford to unmake.”

Carys’s thumb pressed a crease into the edge of the silk bolt and left it there. The first wish had kept the line from fracturing when my father left. The second had brought back a fragment of what the Becoming had taken from Julian. Either one undone would cost more than either of us had left to give.

I realized that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in. If only…

The market stall’s canvas roof snapped in the wind off the Ascendant Run, and Carys’s hand hovered above the folded note I still held between my fingers. I could not make myself release it. The youth’s binding still flickered in my mind, the elder’s demand still pressed at the back of my throat, and every breath I took tasted of the spiralgrass crushed underfoot. Carys leaned closer, her voice low so the other vendors would not hear.

“If you keep it any longer the ink will smudge from your sweat. Give it over.”

My thumb traced the edge of the parchment once more. The note carried the only proof we had that the bloodline geas had been tampered with before the youth ever stepped into the circle. Handing it across meant someone else would know what Julian had already risked to shield us both. I let the paper slide from my palm. Carys took it without flourish, tucking it beneath a bolt of dyed river-silk as though it were nothing more than a price list. Her heel tapped once against the stall leg before she shifted her weight. Behind us the crowd thickened at the next stall. A voice rose above the rest—clear, carrying, the sort that belonged to someone used to being listened to. The council messenger who had arrived at the clearing was reading from a sealed letter, the one that had been intercepted with the token from Julian’s house. The words carried across the market air.

“…three wishes offered in the old manner, each bound to the same bloodline, each paid for in secret. The first for safety of the line, the second for the return of what was lost, the third—”

The rest was lost beneath the sudden rush of voices. People turned. Some laughed, thinking it theater. Others went still, because the old manner meant sacrifice that could not be undone. A fly settled on the back of my wrist and stayed there. Carys’s fingers tightened on the silk.

“They will trace it back,” she said.

“You need to decide which one you can afford to unmake.”

Carys’s thumb pressed a crease into the edge of the silk bolt and left it there. The first wish had kept the line from fracturing when my father left. The second had brought back a fragment of what the Becoming had taken from Julian. Either one undone would cost more than either of us had left to give. Present. If only… Julian's first love, who had returned and was exploiting the very wishes that bound their fates, lingered at the edge of my thoughts. The tension between us was palpable, a reminder of the fractured bond we once shared, now a battleground for legitimacy and control. As the crowd buzzed around us, I couldn't shake the feeling that her presence would tip the scales in ways we were not yet prepared to face.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in. If only…
